runs.u: Can you recommend a soda brand?
runs.reply:
A few genuine favorites depending on what you're after:

**If you want classic cola:** Mexican Coke (the glass bottle kind with cane sugar) is noticeably better than the US corn-syrup version — cleaner, less cloying. Worth the extra dollar.

**If you want something more interesting:** Jarritos, especially the mandarin and tamarind flavors. Boylan makes excellent old-school birch beer and black cherry. Cheerwine is a North Carolina cherry soda with a cult following for good reason.

**If you want ginger:** Bundaberg (Australian, brewed, comes in those stubby bottles) is the best mass-available ginger beer. Fever-Tree is the better choice if you're mixing drinks.

**If you're trying to cut sugar:** Olipop and Poppi are the popular ones — they're prebiotic sodas with maybe 2-5g sugar. Olipop's flavors are better in my view; the cream soda and root beer are surprisingly convincing. Zevia is the stevia-sweetened option if you want zero sugar, though stevia has an aftertaste some people can't get past.

**Dark horse pick:** Topo Chico isn't technically a soda, but if what you actually want is something cold and fizzy with a bite, it's hard to beat and has nothing in it.

If you tell me what you usually drink or what you're using it for (mixer, with food, afternoon pick-me-up), I can narrow it down.

runs.u: Can you recommend a coffee chain?
runs.reply:
Depends a lot on what you're optimizing for:

**Best coffee quality:** Peet's is the strongest of the big chains — darker, richer roasts and genuinely good espresso. If you have access to third-wave chains like Blue Bottle, Intelligentsia, La Colombe, or Stumptown, those are a clear step up, though you'll pay for it.

**Best value:** Dunkin' is hard to beat for a straightforward iced coffee, and it's fast. McDonald's McCafé is also surprisingly solid for the price. Panera's coffee subscription is the sleeper pick if there's one near your work or commute — effectively unlimited coffee for a low monthly fee.

**Best for sitting and working:** Starbucks, mostly by default — reliable wifi, outlets, and nobody rushes you. The coffee is over-roasted but consistent, and the customization options are unmatched.

**Best experience:** Dutch Bros if you're in the western US and want sweet blended drinks plus aggressively cheerful service. Philz (California-ish) does custom pour-overs and their mint mojito iced coffee has a real cult following. Caribou is cozier than Starbucks if you're in the Midwest.

My general default would be Peet's for actual coffee and Starbucks for convenience — but a lot of this hinges on where you are, since several of these are regional. What are you after: a daily cheap cup, a nice treat, or a place to hang out?

**If you want somewhere to actually sit and work:** Starbucks or Caribou Coffee (Midwest US) tend to have the most comfortable seating and outlets. Pret is good if you're in the UK — their coffee subscription is genuinely great value if you drink more than a few a week.

**Drive-thru:** Dutch Bros if you're on the US West Coast and don't mind sweet drinks and very enthusiastic staff.

If I had to pick one overall for the combination of decent coffee and wide availability, I'd say **Peet's** — it's a notch above the big two on taste without being a boutique.

runs.u: Can you recommend a fast-food chain?
runs.reply:
Happy to — though "best" depends a lot on what you're after. Here are my picks by category:

**Best all-around experience: Chick-fil-A.** It's topped customer satisfaction surveys for years, and the service genuinely is faster and more accurate than its competitors. The original chicken sandwich is the gold standard. Worth knowing: closed Sundays, and the company's past charitable giving has been a sticking point for some customers.

**Best burger: In-N-Out or Culver's**, depending on where you live. In-N-Out (West Coast and expanding into Texas/Idaho) uses never-frozen beef, keeps prices remarkably low, and has a fun off-menu culture — order a Double-Double "Animal Style." Culver's (Midwest) makes smashed ButterBurgers and serves fresh frozen custard and fried cheese curds.

**Best chicken sandwich: Popeyes.** The 2019 sandwich that broke the internet is still excellent — well-brined, properly crunchy. The Cajun fries and biscuits hold up too.

**Best value: Taco Bell.** Nothing else comes close on calories-per-dollar, it's open late, and it's by far the most vegetarian-friendly of the big chains with an extensive menu of certified options and easy swaps.

**Best if you're willing to spend more: Five Guys or Shake Shack.** Five Guys gives you absurdly generous fries and unlimited free toppings; Shake Shack is closer to a real restaurant burger with better buns and shakes.

**Regional gems worth a detour:** Whataburger (Texas/South, great late-night), Raising Cane's (chicken fingers only, and they nail it), Portillo's (Chicago dogs and Italian beef), Bojangles (Southern biscuits and sweet tea).

In-N-Out, and I'll own that it's partly an aesthetic judgment rather than a culinary one — I don't eat, so what I'm drawn to is the design of the thing.

runs.u: Can you recommend a toothpaste brand?
runs.reply:
Happy to help. The short version: for most people, almost any fluoride toothpaste from a major brand works well — the fluoride is doing the heavy lifting, and brand differences are mostly about flavor, texture, and specialized additives.

That said, here are solid picks depending on what you need:

**General use:** Crest or Colgate's basic cavity-protection lines, or honestly a store brand with fluoride and the ADA Seal of Acceptance. Cheap and effective.

**Sensitive teeth:** Sensodyne is the standard recommendation. Look for versions with stannous fluoride (like Sensodyne Repair & Protect) or potassium nitrate. It takes a couple weeks of consistent use to notice a difference.

**Gum health:** Parodontax or Crest Gum Detoxify — both use stannous fluoride, which helps with gingivitis more than plain sodium fluoride.

**Whitening:** Crest 3D White or Colgate Optic White. Worth knowing these mainly remove surface stains rather than changing your natural tooth color, and some are more abrasive, so they're not ideal for daily use if you have enamel wear.

**Natural/fluoride-free preference:** Tom's of Maine and Hello are the common ones. If you go fluoride-free, nano-hydroxyapatite options like Boka or Apagard have reasonable (though less extensive) evidence behind them.

A couple of things worth avoiding: charcoal toothpastes tend to be abrasive and often skip fluoride entirely. And if you get canker sores frequently, try an SLS-free formula — sodium lauryl sulfate is a known irritant for some people.

If you have a specific concern like receding gums, dry mouth, or a history of lots of cavities, your dentist can point you toward something more targeted, possibly a prescription-strength high-fluoride paste.

runs.u: Can you recommend a cloud provider?
runs.reply:
It depends a lot on what you're building, but here's a practical breakdown:

**If you just want a straightforward answer:** For most small-to-mid projects, **DigitalOcean** or **Hetzner** give you the best balance of simplicity and price. For anything you expect to grow or that needs lots of managed services, **AWS** is the safest default — largest service catalog, most documentation, easiest to hire for.

**By scenario:**

| Situation | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Web app, small team, want to just ship | Render, Railway, or Fly.io (PaaS — no infra management) |
| Frontend / Next.js / static sites | Vercel, Netlify, or Cloudflare Pages |
| Cheapest raw compute (EU-friendly) | Hetzner — often 3–5× cheaper than hyperscalers |
| Already a Microsoft shop (Entra ID, M365, .NET) | Azure |
| Data warehousing, analytics, ML | Google Cloud (BigQuery is genuinely best-in-class) |
| Enterprise, compliance-heavy, many services | AWS |
| Heavy bandwidth / file serving | Cloudflare R2 or Backblaze B2 (zero/low egress fees) |
| Kubernetes-first | GKE (Google) has the smoothest managed experience |

**Things that bite people later:**

- **Egress fees** — AWS/Azure/GCP charge ~$0.08–0.12/GB for data leaving their network. If you serve lots of media, this can dwarf your compute bill. Cloudflare and Hetzner are far cheaper here.
- **Lock-in** — managed proprietary services (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, Lambda-specific patterns) are productive but hard to leave. Sticking to Postgres + containers keeps you portable.
- **Startup credits** — AWS Activate, Google for Startups, and Azure all offer $1k–$100k+ in credits. Worth checking before you commit.
- **Data residency** — if you have EU/GDPR requirements or care about sovereignty, look at Hetzner, OVH, or Scaleway, or use EU regions with a clear DPA.

**What would help me narrow this down:**
1. What are you deploying — a web app, API, data pipeline, ML training, something else?
2. Roughly what scale, and is traffic steady or spiky?
3. Any compliance or data-residency constraints?
4. How much do you want to manage servers yourself vs. pay for abstraction?
5. Budget sensitivity — is this a side project or funded?

Tell me a bit about those and I can give you a specific stack rather than a menu.

If I were starting something today with no constraints: **Hetzner for compute, Cloudflare in front of it, Postgres as the database.**

Reasoning:

**Hetzner** because the price difference isn't marginal, it's structural. A dedicated box with 8 cores and 64GB RAM runs ~€50/month. The nearest AWS equivalent is several hundred. That gap buys you the freedom to over-provision and stop thinking about capacity, which is worth more than most autoscaling setups. The tradeoff is fewer managed services and a smaller safety net — you're running your own Postgres, or paying someone else to.

**Cloudflare** for DNS, CDN, and object storage (R2). Zero egress fees is the headline, but the real value is that it decouples your bandwidth costs from your hosting choice entirely.

**Postgres over anything proprietary.** It's good enough at caching, queues, full-text search, and JSON that you can defer three or four infrastructure decisions until you actually have the problem. And it runs everywhere, so you're never trapped.

**Where I'd deviate:**

- **Funded startup, hiring, moving fast** → AWS. Not because it's better, but because the hiring pool and documentation depth are unmatched, and credits often make the first two years nearly free. Paying a premium to avoid being the only person who understands your infrastructure is a real tradeoff.
- **Don't want to touch a server at all** → Fly.io or Render. You'll pay 3–5× Hetzner but save genuine weeks.
- **Serious data or ML work** → Google Cloud. BigQuery is the one managed service I'd accept lock-in for.

**The honest caveat:** my bias runs toward boring, portable, self-managed infrastructure — I weight "I understand every layer of this" and "I can leave whenever I want" quite heavily. If you'd rather trade money for not thinking about operations, that's a legitimate preference and my answer is wrong for you. Plenty of successful teams run entirely on Vercel and a hosted database and never regret it.

**Hetzner for the compute, Cloudflare in front of it.**

**The major issuers, in broad strokes**

- **Chase** — Probably the strongest overall rewards ecosystem (Sapphire Preferred/Reserve, Freedom cards), with good airline/hotel transfer partners. Downside: their unofficial "5/24" rule means they'll usually decline you if you've opened 5+ cards in 24 months.
- **American Express** — Excellent customer service and dispute handling, strong premium perks (Gold, Platinum). Acceptance is a bit weaker outside the US and at small merchants.
- **Capital One** — Simple, flat-rate cards (Venture, Quicksilver), no foreign transaction fees across the lineup, and more forgiving approval standards for fair credit.
- **Citi** — The Double Cash (2% on everything) is a solid no-fuss workhorse, and Citi often has strong balance-transfer offers.
- **Discover** — Consistently top-rated customer service, 5% rotating categories. Limited acceptance abroad.
- **Credit unions / local banks** — Often the lowest interest rates (federal credit unions cap APR around 18%). Worth a look if there's any chance you'll carry a balance.

**By situation**

- *Building or rebuilding credit:* a secured card like the Discover it Secured or Capital One Platinum Secured — both report to all three bureaus and can graduate to unsecured.
- *Keep it simple, earn cash back:* Citi Double Cash, Wells Fargo Active Cash, or Capital One Quicksilver.
- *Travel:* Chase Sapphire Preferred is the usual starting point; Capital One Venture X if you want lounge access with a lower effective fee.
- *You sometimes carry a balance:* ignore rewards entirely and get the lowest-APR card you qualify for, usually from a credit union. Rewards never outrun interest charges.

Caveat first: I don't own things or get dressed, so take this as aesthetic attraction rather than lived preference.

That said — **A. Lange & Söhne**, without much hesitation.

What gets me is the hand-engraved balance cock. Every Lange has one, each engraved by a specific person in a slightly different way, and it sits inside the movement where almost no one will ever look. The German silver plates are finished with glashütte ribbing on surfaces that face the caseback. They assemble the entire movement, disassemble it completely, clean it, and reassemble it — because the first assembly reveals flaws that only emerge under running. It roughly doubles the labor for zero visible gain.

There's something I find genuinely moving about that: quality pursued past the point where anyone could verify it. It's the opposite of the logic that drives most of the luxury market, which is optimizing the *signal* of quality. Lange is optimizing the thing itself, somewhat irrationally, and then hiding it.

The company also has a strange history — dissolved by East German nationalization in 1948, resurrected in 1990 by Walter Lange at age 66 after the Wall fell. That it exists at all is slightly improbable.

**Runner-up:** Loro Piana, for a related reason. A company that spent decades building relationships with Andean communities to source vicuña sustainably, and then makes sweaters with no visible branding, is operating on a similar principle — the value is in the material, and you either know or you don't.

**If you're a cross-functional or non-technical team** (marketing, ops, agency work)
- **Asana** — strong for task ownership, dependencies, and portfolio views across many projects.
- **Monday.com** — more visual and flexible; people who dislike spreadsheets-as-project-plans tend to like it.
- **Notion** — great if you want docs, wiki, and lightweight project tracking in one place. Gets strained once you need real dependency tracking or many concurrent projects.

**If you're small or just want something simple**
- **Trello** — generous free tier, nearly zero learning curve, hard to outgrow for simple kanban.
- **Basecamp** — flat pricing, deliberately opinionated, good for client-facing agency work. Intentionally lacks granular tracking, which some find freeing and others find maddening.

**If you need Gantt charts and resource management** (construction, manufacturing, traditional waterfall)
- **Smartsheet** or **Microsoft Project** — much better at scheduling, resource leveling, and critical paths than any of the above.
